afd.text:
000
FXUS65 KPSR 271152
AFDPSR

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Phoenix AZ
452 AM MST Fri Nov 27 2026

.UPDATE...Updated 12Z Aviation Discussion.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Dry and tranquil weather will prevail through early next week 
  with temperatures hovering slightly above normal for late 
  November.

- A Pacific low is expected to track through the Desert Southwest
  during the middle of next week, leading to a period with gusty 
  winds, rain chances, and cooler temperatures.

&&

.SHORT TERM /TODAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
A well-defined, compact cyclonic circulation is apparent in 
midlevel water vapor imagery at this hour, departing the vicinity 
of Hawaii to the northeast. A prominent ridge sits downstream of 
this feature, encompassing the forecast area under its eastern 
periphery and bringing northwesterly, anticyclonic flow aloft. As 
the ridge nudges slightly further east today, heights/temperatures
aloft will likely peak at their highest values for the 
foreseeable future. NAEFS/ENS mean H5 heights are forecast to peak
around 586 dam (eastern CWA) to 590 dam (western CWA), between 
the 95th-99th percentiles of climatology for late November, while 
850 mb temperatures warm to 17C- 20C this afternoon, also around 
the 95th-99th percentiles. Despite the unusually warm temperatures
aloft, better anticyclonic subsidence will be confined offshore 
the SoCal Coast, and periods of thicker high clouds will help to 
moderate surface temperatures. As a result, anticipate afternoon 
highs only 5F-8F above daily normals today, between the middle 70s
to around 80F across the lower deserts. 

This weekend, ensembles remain in excellent agreement that 
prominent ridging/anticyclonic flow aloft will transition to 
quasi-zonal flow, leading to gradually decreasing heights aloft. 
However, the relatively warm air mass in place over the forecast 
area will not be entirely eroded/displaced, and so temperatures 
will continue to fluctuate day to day in a slightly above normal 
range. Thick high clouds on Saturday, indicated by REFS guidance 
and GFS bufr soundings, may prevent temperatures from exceeding 
the middle 70s across the lower deserts. This is reflected in the 
latest NBM highs, which have come down a few degrees for Saturday.
Lower desert highs should then return to near 80F for the 
typically warmer spots on Sunday as the thicker cirrus decks 
depart. 

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...    
Relatively quiet weather should continue into the beginning of 
next week as quasi-zonal flow aloft continues. However, a building
SLP gradient across the the Baja Spine/San Diego Mountains could 
begin to induce strong westerly gap winds in the typically prone 
I-8 corridor near Mountain Springs as early as Sunday night/early 
Monday morning. Otherwise, generally light winds and afternoon 
highs in the middle 70s across the lower deserts should prevail 
Monday.

There is building model consensus in a potent Pacific trough 
developing off the West Coast early next week, which will then 
progress through the Southwest US during the middle of the week. A
large majority of ensemble members now show the trough digging 
far enough south to pull decent moisture into the region - 
overall, a favorable trajectory to support rain if ascent 
mechanisms align. The evolution of this system is just now 
starting to come into better focus. The latest global guidance is 
in decent agreement that rain chances will likely come in 2 
separate periods, one associated with an initial Pacific cold 
front with WAA/saturated isentropic ascent in a narrow band out 
ahead of it and a more concentrated area of frontogenetical 
forcing trailing behind, followed by a second period likely 
sometime on Wednesday associated with the passage of the center of
the upper low. These details are certainly subject to change.

Rainfall potential is still highly uncertain this far out, but 
WPC QPF has trended up once again in the latest update, now 
showing average rain totals on the order of 0.75-1.00" across the 
South- Central AZ lower deserts through the entire event. As is 
typical, there is a strong gradient towards the higher terrain to 
the north and east of Phoenix, a consequence of orographic 
enhancement. Experience suggests that rain shadowing effects are 
underplayed in the WPC QPF for far Southwest AZ and Southeast CA, 
and so the totals out there may underperform compared to the 
current forecast (average totals between 0.20-0.50"). Some 
isolated/embedded thunderstorm activity cannot be ruled out during
this event, with the most likely timing coinciding with the first
period, along/ahead of the front. Model soundings currently 
indicate weak instability (100-250 J/kg MUCAPE) at this time, but 
if cooler air aloft moves in quickly enough, lapse rates may 
become more favorable. The coldest air aloft will come with the 
passage of the upper low on Wednesday, but moisture profiles do 
not look as robust, and the exact track of the low will determine 
where this "second period" of precipitation sets up. Aside from 
rain chances, widespread gusty winds will be a concern with this 
upcoming system. Height packing ahead of the trough and a 
cyclonically curved attendant jet streak will support deep, strong
southwesterly flow. Mixing during the afternoon on Tuesday should
tap this higher momentum air, resulting in gusts between 25-40 
mph across the lower deserts, locally higher over ridgetops. Model
consensus currently shows the front passing through Tuesday 
night, such that by Wednesday, gradients will begin to relax, and 
only lingering breeziness should remain for some areas. 

By Thursday, the Pacific low will have weakened substantially and 
progressed east of the region, allowing an opportunity for quick 
clearing and a period with weak temperature/pressure gradients 
across the region. Light winds and widespread wetting rainfall could 
set the stage for fog to develop across portions of the lower 
deserts, but this will be highly dependent on cloud cover. 
Regardless, cooler temperatures behind the front will prevail 
starting Wednesday, with latest NBM showing temperatures dropping 
close to daily normals. A period of quieter weather should follow 
the passage of this Pacific trough, though the active pattern may 
soon return thereafter (potentially by the weekend).

&&

.AVIATION...Updated at 1150Z.

South Central Arizona including KPHX, KIWA, KSDL, and KDVT;
Southeast California/Southwest Arizona including KIPL and KBLH:
 
Light winds will prevail through Saturday morning, with 
directions following typical diurnal trends. Extended periods of 
light variability to calm conditions are also expected. High 
cirrus will pass over the area through the TAF period.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER... 
Dry and generally tranquil conditions will prevail through the
beginning of next week. Temperatures will be fairly stable during
this time in a 3F-9F above normal range. Afternoon minimum 
humidities will vary between 15-25% areawide following fair to 
good overnight recoveries between 30-60% through the weekend. 
Humidity will then improve through the middle of next week. A 
weather system will result in increasing southerly to 
southwesterly winds, especially by Tuesday, and increased chances 
for wetting rain and possibly some isolated/embedded 
thunderstorms. Until then, anticipate winds to be light, mostly 
below 15 mph.

&&

.HYDROLOGY...Updated 11/27 1020Z.
Gila River: A Flood Warning remains in effect from Painted Rock 
Dam through the Dateland area due to continued flow in the Gila 
River, however, upstream releases have ceased. Water levels near 
Dateland have begun to decrease, with gauge data now showing a 
stage of 6.7 ft and flow around 620 cfs. A separate Flood Warning 
segment remains in effect from Dateland to Yuma. These water 
levels will have the potential to flood farm fields and low water 
crossings along the river downstream from the dam. The downstream 
gauge near Dome has yet to respond. 

&&

.PSR WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
AZ...None.
CA...None.
&&

$$

SHORT TERM...Whittock
LONG TERM...Whittock
AVIATION...Benedict
FIRE WEATHER...Whittock
HYDROLOGY...Whittock
